title: How to understand Repo vs Rev Repo so that can remember them easily in balance sheet?
summary: I am a data engineer in Finance. Recently I am suffering from understanding financial terms and its accounting treatment. One big issue is, as a frequently used term, Repo and Rev Repo I understand them several times, but after a period not touching the terms and related data I will forget almost all of the details. And then have to revisit the definitions and relink them to financial activities. For example, recently I am involved in a meeting talking about Repo Fails transactions. User wants to know what’s the exact accounting policy we applied in our data logic. My first reaction is, how to identify the Repo in our Fails data, however, Fails will only record as Fail to deliver or Fail to receive. The only way to find a Repo is from the trading account. We maintain certain accounts for Repo trade only. Question is I even can’t have a clear filter to scope which accounts are Repo or not. It takes me almost a whole day to look into firm’s internal documentation to understand what the user means and how our data pipeline process it. Then, with these background, I joined the meeting. In the meeting, I listened carefully but didn’t fully comprehend what the user means as lot’s of non Tech terms. Fortunately I got something like below For a repo trade how it is recorded in accounting On Trade date (T0) Dr (i.e., Assets in BS): Repo Cr (i.e. Liabilities in BS): Rev Repo On T1 if settled successfully Dr: Receivables ??? Cr: Cash ??? On T1 if settlement failed Dr: Failed to Deliver Cr: Payables On TX(usually no longer than 5 calendar days) if settlement success Dr: Receivables Cr: Cash This time my understanding for memory: Repo means repurchase, we should provide securities to the client and client give us money. And by someday (possibly overnight), we need to return the money + interest to client. So the money measured assets is still on our side on trade date. We recorded an assets repo and liabilities Rev repo. If not failed, user doesn’t mentioned. If failed, we faile

title: How to Organize Your Email Inbox (And Keep it That Way!)
summary: Want to organize your inbox without spending hours sorting email? I’ll walk through five practical Outlook tips to reduce clutter, keep track of follow-ups, and find the messages that actually need your attention. Then I’ll show you how Superhuman Mail uses AI to make organization even easier and help you achieve Inbox Zero! 🎁 Try Superhuman Mail: Superhuman Mail is celebrating Inbox Zero Day on October 6! New users who sign up through October 16 can get two months free at https://superhuman.com/elizabeth An overflowing inbox can make every message feel equally urgent. Newsletters sit beside client requests; reminders get buried, and emails you’ve already handled stay in your way. You don’t need a complicated system to fix that. A few useful Outlook features and consistent habits can make a big difference. In this video, you’ll learn how to: - Create Outlook Rules that automatically move or prioritize incoming emails - Use Categories to see what needs action, what’s important, and what you’re waiting on - Flag and snooze messages instead of marking them unread as a reminder - Set up Quick Steps to handle repetitive email tasks with one click - Archive completed emails while keeping them searchable After the Outlook tips, we’ll explore Superhuman Mail. I’ll show you how features like Auto Labels, Auto Archive, and Split Inbox can help separate important conversations from newsletters, notifications, and promotions. We’ll also look at Auto Reminders and Auto Drafts, which can help you follow up without keeping every unanswered conversation in your inbox. The goal isn’t necessarily to reach Inbox Zero every day. It’s to build an email workflow that helps you see what matters, take action, and trust that follow-ups won’t be forgotten.
